text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- More and more people work overtime for no pay, particularly men employed by the government, research by professor Gunnar Aronsson shows. Every third state-employed administrator works overtime at least five hours a week.
- Swedish automotive group Volvo expects to invest two billion crowns in the longterm in heavy vehicles in India. The group has just started building a truck plant outside Bangalore.

- Prime Minister Goran Persson said he is one of the only ones who believes the government will meet its goal of halving unemployment to four percent by the year 2000. However, he said the target is still within reach.
- Sweden's Kolmarden zoo is considering alternatives including selling animals and bankruptcy because of heavy debt.
- Blue-collar union Metall would like the government to give a cautious nod to Europe's economic and monetary union.
- The state is waiting for the right buyer for its 25 percent stake in information technology company Enator and says finding the right one is more important than the price the stake fetches.

- Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, has miscalculated how much foreign shares Swedes have been buying from 1994 to January 1997. Its new data show Swedes bought foreign shares for 27.4 billion crowns more than previously thought.
- Swedish drugs major Astra calls for support to pressure third world countries to respect its patents because it says global patents are extremely important for its future.

- Large Swedish companies account poorly for financial effects of environmental issues. For example, not one of 28 new annual reports posted allowances for costs related to recycling products or packaging.
